cards.q: Define electric current.
cards.a: The rate of flow of charge: \(I = \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t}\).
cards.why: One ampere is one coulomb of charge passing a point each second.

cards.q: Define the potential difference between two points.
cards.a: The work done (energy transferred) per unit charge moving between the two points: \(V = \frac{W}{Q}\).
cards.why: Say "per unit charge", not "per coulomb": a definition should not rely on a particular unit.

cards.q: Define the resistance of a component.
cards.a: The ratio of the potential difference across it to the current in it: \(R = \frac{V}{I}\).
cards.why: This definition holds for every component, ohmic or not.

cards.q: State Ohm's law.
cards.a: The current in a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided the temperature (physical conditions) stays constant.
cards.why: The condition earns a mark: without constant temperature the proportionality fails.

cards.q: A student writes: "Ohm's law is \(R = \frac{V}{I}\)." What is wrong with this?
cards.a: \(R = \frac{V}{I}\) is the definition of resistance and applies to any component. Ohm's law is the statement that \(I \propto V\) at constant temperature, which is true only for ohmic conductors.
cards.why: A filament lamp has a resistance \(\frac{V}{I}\) at every point on its curve, but it does not obey Ohm's law.

cards.q: Express the volt in terms of the joule and the coulomb.
cards.why: It follows directly from \(V = \frac{W}{Q}\).

cards.q: A current of 0.25 A flows for 2.0 minutes. Calculate the charge that passes.
cards.a: 30 C
cards.why: The usual slip is leaving the time in minutes.

cards.q: A charge of 30 C passes through a lamp. How many electrons is this? (\(e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}\))
cards.a: \(1.9 \times 10^{20}\) electrons
steps: Each electron carries a charge of magnitude \(e\), so \(N = \frac{Q}{e}\).

cards.q: 5.0 C of charge passes through a resistor with a potential difference of 12 V across it. Calculate the energy transferred.
cards.a: 60 J

cards.q: Describe the current–potential difference graph of an ohmic conductor at constant temperature.
cards.a: A straight line through the origin, continuing in the same line for negative values.
cards.why: Straight and through the origin together mean \(I \propto V\), so the resistance is constant.

answerFigure.alt: Current against potential difference for an ohmic conductor: a straight line through the origin, continuing in the same way for negative values.

cards.q: Describe the shape of the \(I\)–\(V\) graph of a filament lamp, with \(I\) on the vertical axis.
cards.a: A curve through the origin whose gradient decreases as \(V\) increases, in both directions (an S-shape through the origin).
cards.why: The curve flattens because the resistance rises as the filament heats up.

answerFigure.alt: Current against potential difference for a filament lamp: a curve through the origin that gets less steep as the potential difference increases, in both directions.

cards.q: Explain why the resistance of a filament lamp increases as the current in it increases.
cards.a: A larger current heats the filament, and a hotter metal has a higher resistance.
marks: The current transfers energy to the filament, so its temperature rises.
The lattice ions vibrate with greater amplitude.
Conduction electrons collide with the ions more frequently.
So a larger potential difference is needed for each unit of current: the resistance increases.

cards.q: Describe the \(I\)–\(V\) characteristic of a semiconductor diode.
cards.a: In the forward direction almost no current flows until a threshold of about 0.6 V (silicon), then the current rises steeply. In the reverse direction the current is almost zero.
cards.why: The diode has a very high resistance in reverse and a low resistance once it conducts in the forward direction.

answerFigure.alt: Current against potential difference for a silicon diode: almost zero current for all negative values and up to about 0.6 volts, then a very steep rise.

cards.q: A student finds the resistance of a filament lamp from the gradient of a tangent to its \(I\)–\(V\) curve. Why is this wrong?
cards.a: Resistance is defined as \(\frac{V}{I}\) at that point: read the two values and divide. The gradient only gives the resistance when the graph is a straight line through the origin.
cards.why: For a curve, the tangent's gradient is \(\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta V}\), which is not \(\frac{I}{V}\).

cards.q: What resistance does an ideal ammeter have, and an ideal voltmeter?
cards.a: An ideal ammeter has zero resistance. An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.
cards.why: Then the ammeter takes no potential difference and the voltmeter takes no current, so neither changes the circuit it measures.

cards.q: A filament lamp's characteristic is drawn with \(V\) on the vertical axis and \(I\) on the horizontal axis. How does the curve bend?
cards.a: It curves upwards: the gradient increases as \(I\) increases.
cards.why: Swapping the axes flips the curve. Check which quantity is on which axis before describing a characteristic.

answerFigure.alt: Potential difference against current for a filament lamp: a curve from the origin that gets steeper as the current increases.

cards.q: Describe the \(I\)–\(V\) graph of an NTC thermistor as the current heats it, with \(I\) on the vertical axis.
cards.a: A curve through the origin whose gradient increases as \(V\) increases.
cards.why: As the thermistor warms, its resistance falls, so each extra volt drives more extra current. It is the opposite of a filament lamp.

answerFigure.alt: Current against potential difference for an NTC thermistor: a curve from the origin that gets steeper as the potential difference increases.

cards.q: Define the resistivity of a material, giving the equation.
cards.a: \(\rho = \frac{RA}{L}\), where \(R\) is the resistance of a sample of length \(L\) and cross-sectional area \(A\). It is a property of the material (at a given temperature), not of the particular wire.

cards.q: State the SI unit of resistivity.
cards.a: The ohm metre, \(\Omega\ \text{m}\).
cards.why: It is ohm times metre, not ohm per metre: \(\frac{RA}{L}\) has units \(\frac{\Omega\ \text{m}^{2}}{\text{m}}\).

cards.q: A copper wire is 2.0 m long with a diameter of 0.50 mm. The resistivity of copper is \(1.7 \times 10^{-8}\ \Omega\ \text{m}\). Calculate its resistance.
cards.a: 0.17 Ω
cards.why: Two common slips: using the diameter as the radius, and leaving millimetres unconverted.

cards.q: A wire has a diameter of 0.40 mm. Calculate its cross-sectional area in \(\text{m}^{2}\).
cards.a: \(1.3 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{2}\)
cards.why: Halve the diameter first, and convert to metres before squaring.

cards.q: A wire is replaced by one of the same material with twice the length and twice the diameter. How does the resistance change?
cards.a: It halves.
steps: Doubling the diameter makes the area four times larger, which divides \(R\) by 4.
cards.why: Area depends on the square of the diameter.

cards.q: Outline how to determine the resistivity of a metal wire.
cards.a: Find the resistance of several different lengths, plot \(R\) against \(L\), and use the gradient with the cross-sectional area.
marks: Measure the diameter with a micrometer at several places and orientations, and take the mean.
Calculate the area from \(A = \frac{\pi d^{2}}{4}\).
For each length \(L\), measure \(V\) and \(I\) and calculate \(R = \frac{V}{I}\).
Plot \(R\) against \(L\): a straight line with gradient \(\frac{\rho}{A}\).
\(\rho = \text{gradient} \times A\).

cards.q: In the resistivity experiment, why is the current kept small and switched off between readings?
cards.a: To stop the wire heating up. A rise in temperature would increase its resistance, so the readings would not all be for the same resistivity.

cards.q: In the resistivity experiment, which measurement usually contributes most to the uncertainty in \(\rho\), and why?
cards.a: The diameter. It is very small, so its percentage uncertainty is large, and because \(A \propto d^{2}\) that percentage uncertainty is doubled.

cards.q: A wire's diameter is measured as \(0.38 \pm 0.01\ \text{mm}\). Calculate the percentage uncertainty in its cross-sectional area.
cards.a: 5.3%
steps: \(A \propto d^{2}\), so the percentage uncertainty doubles.
cards.why: When a quantity is raised to a power, multiply its percentage uncertainty by that power.

cards.q: A graph of \(R\) against \(L\) for a wire is a straight line that does not pass through the origin. Suggest a cause, and state whether it affects the value of \(\rho\).
cards.a: A systematic error, such as contact resistance at the clips or a zero error in the length. It shifts every point by the same amount, so the gradient, and therefore \(\rho\), is unaffected.
cards.why: This is why the gradient is used, not a single pair of readings.

cards.q: Explain why the resistance of a metal conductor increases when its temperature rises.
cards.a: The lattice ions vibrate more, so conduction electrons collide with them more often.
marks: The positive ions of the lattice vibrate with greater amplitude at a higher temperature.
Conduction electrons collide with the ions more frequently.
The number of conduction electrons stays about the same, so the current for a given potential difference falls: resistance increases.

cards.q: How does the resistance of an NTC thermistor change as its temperature rises, and why?
cards.a: Its resistance decreases.
marks: Heating gives electrons enough energy to break free, so the number of conduction electrons increases greatly.
The lattice vibrations also increase, which on its own would raise the resistance.
The increase in the number of charge carriers has the larger effect, so the resistance falls.
cards.why: NTC stands for negative temperature coefficient.

aqa.note: AQA asks for the qualitative effect; the explanation is useful support.

cards.q: Describe the resistance–temperature graph of an NTC thermistor.
cards.a: A curve that falls as temperature rises: steep at low temperatures and levelling off at high temperatures. It is not a straight line.

answerFigure.alt: Resistance against temperature for an NTC thermistor: the resistance falls steeply at first as the temperature rises, then more and more gradually.

cards.q: What is a superconductor?
cards.a: A material that has zero resistivity at and below a critical temperature.
cards.why: The critical temperature depends on the material.

cards.q: Give two applications of superconductors.
cards.a: Producing strong magnetic fields (very large currents with no heating), and reducing energy loss in the transmission of electric power.

cards.q: In \(I = nqvA\), what does each symbol stand for?
cards.a: \(I\): current. \(n\): number of charge carriers per unit volume. \(q\): charge on each carrier. \(v\): drift velocity of the carriers. \(A\): cross-sectional area of the conductor.
cards.why: \(n\) is a number density, with unit \(\text{m}^{-3}\): it is not the total number of carriers.

cards.q: Use \(I = nqvA\) to explain why metals, semiconductors and insulators have such different resistivities.
cards.a: They differ enormously in \(n\), the number of charge carriers per unit volume.
marks: Metals have a very large \(n\) (about one or more free electrons per atom), so a large current flows for a given drift velocity: low resistivity.
Semiconductors have a much smaller \(n\), so their resistivity is much higher.
Insulators have almost no free charge carriers, so \(n\) is negligible and the resistivity is extremely high.

cards.q: A copper wire of cross-sectional area \(1.0 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^{2}\) carries a current of 2.0 A. Copper has \(8.5 \times 10^{28}\) free electrons per \(\text{m}^{3}\). Calculate the drift velocity. (\(e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}\))
cards.a: \(1.5 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)
cards.why: Drift velocities are tiny, a fraction of a millimetre per second, even for large currents.

cards.q: How does the resistance of a light dependent resistor (LDR) change as the light intensity on it increases?
cards.a: Its resistance decreases.
cards.why: Light releases more conduction electrons in the semiconductor, so there are more charge carriers.

cards.q: The total current entering a junction equals the total current leaving it. Which conservation law is this a consequence of?
cards.a: Conservation of charge.
cards.why: Charge cannot build up or disappear at a junction, so what flows in each second must flow out.

cards.q: Around any closed loop of a circuit, the sum of the emfs equals the sum of the potential differences. Which conservation law is this a consequence of?
cards.a: Conservation of energy.
cards.why: The energy given to each unit of charge by the sources equals the energy it transfers in the components round the loop.

cards.q: State the equations for the total resistance of resistors in series, and in parallel.

edexcel.note: Not on the Edexcel formulae sheet: you must know these and be able to derive them.

cards.q: Derive the equation for the total resistance of two resistors in series.
steps: Conservation of charge: the same current \(I\) is in both resistors.
Conservation of energy: the total potential difference is the sum, \(V = V_{1} + V_{2}\).
Use \(V = IR\) for each: \(IR_{T} = IR_{1} + IR_{2}\).

cards.q: Derive the equation for the total resistance of two resistors in parallel.
steps: Conservation of energy: the potential difference \(V\) is the same across both resistors.
Conservation of charge: the total current is the sum, \(I = I_{1} + I_{2}\).

cards.q: Calculate the total resistance of a 6.0 Ω resistor and a 3.0 Ω resistor connected in parallel.
cards.a: 2.0 Ω
cards.why: The usual slip is forgetting the final reciprocal and giving 0.50 Ω.

cards.q: How does the total resistance of resistors in parallel compare with the smallest individual resistance?
cards.a: It is always less than the smallest one.
cards.why: Each added branch is an extra route for charge, so more current flows for the same potential difference. Use this to check a calculated answer.

cards.q: A 12 V supply of negligible internal resistance is connected to a 4.0 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 6.0 Ω and 3.0 Ω. Calculate the potential difference across the parallel pair.
cards.a: 4.0 V
steps: Potential difference across the pair: \(V = IR = 2.0 \times 2.0 = 4.0\ \text{V}\).
cards.why: Check: the 4.0 Ω resistor takes 8.0 V, and 8.0 + 4.0 = 12 V.

cards.q: Two different resistors are connected in series. Which form of the power equation shows most directly which one dissipates more power: \(P = I^{2}R\) or \(P = \frac{V^{2}}{R}\)?
cards.a: \(P = I^{2}R\). In series the current is the same in both, so the larger resistance dissipates more power.
cards.why: In parallel the potential difference is the same, so use \(P = \frac{V^{2}}{R}\): there the smaller resistance dissipates more.

cards.q: Starting from \(P = VI\), derive \(P = I^{2}R\) and \(P = \frac{V^{2}}{R}\).
cards.a: Substitute \(V = IR\), then \(I = \frac{V}{R}\).

cards.q: A heater takes a current of 8.7 A from a 230 V supply. Calculate the energy it transfers in 3.0 minutes.
cards.a: \(3.6 \times 10^{5}\ \text{J}\)

aqa.note: \(E = IVt\) is not on the AQA formulae sheet: build it from \(P = IV\) and \(E = Pt\).

cards.q: A student says: "Current gets used up as it goes through a lamp." Correct this.
cards.a: The current is the same on both sides of the lamp, because charge is conserved. What the lamp takes from the charge is energy: each unit of charge leaves with less electrical potential energy.

cards.q: Three cells, each of emf 1.5 V, are connected in series in the same direction. What is the total emf, and what happens to the internal resistance?
cards.a: The total emf is 4.5 V: emfs in series add. The internal resistances also add.

cards.q: Two identical cells, each of emf \(\varepsilon\) and internal resistance \(r\), are connected in parallel. State the emf and the internal resistance of the combination.
cards.a: The emf is still \(\varepsilon\). The internal resistance is \(\frac{r}{2}\).
cards.why: Each cell supplies half the current, so the combination lasts longer and loses fewer volts, but it does not push any harder.

cards.q: A student says: "In a parallel circuit the current takes the path of least resistance." Correct this.
cards.a: Every branch carries current. The current divides so that the branch with the smaller resistance carries the larger share: the currents are in the inverse ratio of the resistances.
cards.why: The potential difference is the same across each branch, so \(I = \frac{V}{R}\) in every one.

cards.q: Two identical lamps are connected in series across a supply. Compared with one lamp alone across the same supply, what power does each lamp now dissipate? Assume the resistance of a lamp stays constant.
cards.a: One quarter of the power.
steps: Each lamp now has half the supply potential difference across it.
\(P = \frac{V^{2}}{R}\), so halving \(V\) gives \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2} = \frac{1}{4}\) of the power.

cards.q: What is a potential divider?
cards.a: Two or more resistors in series across a supply, which share the supply potential difference in proportion to their resistances.
cards.why: The same current is in each, and \(V = IR\), so the larger resistance takes the larger share.

cards.q: Resistors \(R_{1}\) and \(R_{2}\) are in series across a supply \(V_{\text{in}}\). Write the equation for the potential difference across \(R_{2}\).
cards.a: \(V_{\text{out}} = V_{\text{in}} \times \frac{R_{2}}{R_{1} + R_{2}}\)
cards.why: The resistor you are finding the potential difference across goes on top.

aqa.note: Not on the AQA formulae sheet.

edexcel.note: Not on the Edexcel formulae sheet.

cards.q: A 4.0 kΩ resistor and a 2.0 kΩ resistor are in series across a 12 V supply. Calculate the potential difference across the 2.0 kΩ resistor.
cards.a: 4.0 V
cards.why: Both resistances are in kilohms, so the ratio needs no conversion.

cards.q: An NTC thermistor and a fixed resistor are in series across a supply. Explain what happens to the potential difference across the fixed resistor when the temperature rises.
cards.a: It increases.
marks: The resistance of the thermistor decreases as the temperature rises.
The thermistor now takes a smaller share of the supply potential difference.
The supply potential difference is unchanged, so the potential difference across the fixed resistor increases.
cards.why: Alternatively: the total resistance falls, the current rises, and \(V = IR\) for the fixed resistor rises.

cards.q: An LDR and a fixed resistor are in series across a supply. A lamp must switch on when it gets dark. Across which component should the switching circuit be connected, and why?
cards.a: Across the LDR.
marks: In the dark the resistance of the LDR increases.
The LDR takes a larger share of the supply potential difference.
The rising potential difference across the LDR can be used to switch the lamp on.

cards.q: Two 10 kΩ resistors are in series across a 12 V supply. A load of resistance 10 kΩ is then connected across one of them. Calculate the potential difference across the load.
cards.a: 4.0 V
steps: The load is in parallel with one 10 kΩ resistor: \(\frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{10}\), so \(R = 5.0\ \text{k}\Omega\).
The divider is now 10 kΩ in series with 5.0 kΩ.
cards.why: Without the load the output would be 6.0 V. Connecting a load lowers the output of a potential divider.

cards.q: A uniform wire carries a steady current. How does the potential difference across a section of the wire depend on the length of that section?
cards.a: It is directly proportional to the length.
cards.why: For a uniform wire, resistance is proportional to length, and the current is the same throughout, so \(V = IR \propto L\).

cards.q: A variable resistor is connected as a potential divider across a supply (three terminals used, output taken from the sliding contact). What range of output potential difference can it give?
cards.a: From zero up to the full supply potential difference.
cards.why: A variable resistor simply placed in series with a component cannot reduce the potential difference across it to zero.

cards.q: Define the electromotive force (emf) of a source.
cards.a: The energy transferred to electrical energy per unit charge passing through the source: \(\varepsilon = \frac{E}{Q}\).
cards.why: It is energy per unit charge, measured in volts. It is not a force.

cards.q: What is meant by the internal resistance of a cell?
cards.a: The resistance of the cell itself to the current passing through it. Some of the energy given to each unit of charge is dissipated inside the cell.

cards.q: What is the terminal potential difference of a cell?
cards.a: The potential difference across the terminals of the cell: the energy per unit charge delivered to the external circuit. \(V = \varepsilon - Ir\).

cards.q: In \(\varepsilon = I(R + r)\), what do the terms \(IR\) and \(Ir\) represent?
cards.a: \(IR\) is the terminal potential difference, across the external resistance \(R\). \(Ir\) is the potential difference across the internal resistance \(r\), often called the lost volts.

edexcel.note: Not on the Edexcel formulae sheet.

cards.q: When is the terminal potential difference of a cell equal to its emf?
cards.a: Only when there is no current in the cell (open circuit). Whenever a current flows, the terminal potential difference is less than the emf by \(Ir\).
cards.why: Examiners report that using the emf as the terminal potential difference is one of the most common errors in circuit questions.

cards.q: A cell of emf 6.0 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω is connected to a 5.5 Ω resistor. Calculate the terminal potential difference.
cards.a: 5.5 V
cards.why: Check: lost volts \(= Ir = 0.50\ \text{V}\), and 6.0 − 0.50 = 5.5 V.

cards.q: A cell has an emf of 1.5 V. When it supplies a current of 0.60 A, its terminal potential difference is 1.2 V. Calculate its internal resistance.
cards.a: 0.50 Ω

cards.q: Outline how to determine the emf and internal resistance of a cell.
cards.a: Measure the terminal potential difference for a range of currents and plot \(V\) against \(I\).
marks: Connect the cell to a variable resistor, with an ammeter in series and a voltmeter across the cell's terminals.
Change the resistance to obtain a range of values of current \(I\) and terminal potential difference \(V\).
Plot \(V\) (vertical axis) against \(I\).
\(V = \varepsilon - Ir\), so the graph is a straight line: the intercept on the \(V\) axis is \(\varepsilon\).
The gradient is \(-r\).

cards.q: For a cell, a graph of terminal potential difference \(V\) against current \(I\) is plotted. What do the intercept on the \(V\) axis and the gradient represent?
cards.a: The intercept is the emf. The gradient is \(-r\): its magnitude is the internal resistance.
cards.why: Compare \(V = -rI + \varepsilon\) with \(y = mx + c\).

answerFigure.alt: Terminal potential difference against current for a cell: a straight line sloping downwards from the e.m.f. on the vertical axis.

cards.q: In the internal resistance experiment, why is the switch opened between readings and large currents avoided?
cards.a: So that the cell does not run down or heat up during the experiment, either of which would change its emf and internal resistance.

cards.q: Explain why a car's headlamps dim when the starter motor is switched on.
cards.a: The battery's terminal potential difference falls because of its internal resistance.
marks: The starter motor draws a very large current from the battery.
The potential difference across the internal resistance (lost volts, \(Ir\)) becomes large.
The terminal potential difference \(V = \varepsilon - Ir\) falls.
The headlamps are connected across the terminals, so they have a smaller potential difference and dissipate less power.

cards.q: A cell of emf \(\varepsilon\) and internal resistance \(r\) is short-circuited by a wire of negligible resistance. What is the current?
cards.a: \(I = \frac{\varepsilon}{r}\). This is the maximum current the cell can supply.
cards.why: With \(R = 0\), \(\varepsilon = I(R + r)\) becomes \(\varepsilon = Ir\). All the energy is dissipated inside the cell.

cards.q: Multiply \(\varepsilon = IR + Ir\) through by \(I\). What does each term of the result represent?
cards.a: \(\varepsilon I = I^{2}R + I^{2}r\). \(\varepsilon I\) is the total power supplied by the cell, \(I^{2}R\) is the power delivered to the external resistance, and \(I^{2}r\) is the power wasted inside the cell.

cards.q: Why does a high-resistance voltmeter connected directly across a cell read a value very close to the cell's emf?
cards.a: The voltmeter draws a negligible current, so the lost volts \(Ir\) are negligible and the terminal potential difference is almost equal to the emf.
